query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, a controlled addition of aluminum (around 5 at%) will promote the in-situ formation of ordered intermetallic precipitates (e.g., gamma-TiAl-like phases) that hinder dislocation motion and thereby enhance elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the base alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents and at least three additional elements in roughly 5–35 at% each, produced by conventional melting and casting methods.
generation.intervention: Introduce an aluminum addition of approximately 5 at% into the alloy during processing.
generation.conditions: Testing under elevated-temperature conditions in the range of 600–800°C, representative of extreme operating environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of finely dispersed, ordered intermetallic precipitates (such as gamma-TiAl-like phases) within the disordered high-entropy matrix.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum acts as a microalloying element that promotes nucleation and growth of ordered intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates serve as obstacles to dislocation motion, leading to precipitation strengthening at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-added alloy will demonstrate significantly improved tensile strength and creep resistance at high temperatures relative to an otherwise identical alloy without the aluminum addition.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (tensile strength, creep resistance) of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without any aluminum addition.
generation.boundary: The alloy must adhere to the high-entropy alloy compositional definition (five or more elements with each present at 5–35 at%) and be tested under temperatures typical for high-temperature structural applications (600–800°C).
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence for the role of aluminum in titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys is lacking; thus, the precise volume fraction of precipitates formed and the optimal aluminum content remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloy samples – one set following the baseline composition (without aluminum) and the other with a 5 at% aluminum addition. Process both sets under identical conditions. Conduct high-temperature tensile and creep tests at 600–800°C. Use phase identification techniques (XRD, TEM) to detect the presence and distribution of any ordered intermetallic precipitates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-added samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in tensile strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures or if no ordered intermetallic precipitates are observed compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
